questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Cylinder
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/658f58654e8791f15fe6c2a9c719de3b02aa1c3912b4b6dc7b4e2fe2d2cdda62.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,(3-z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $3$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,(3-z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/05664db64ac6595ff0caec7daeec20cb3508d5c18a5266aa126295e3aa040233.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,(3-3)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,(3-z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,(3-0)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-3\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-3\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =-3{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-3\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-6\pi \cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =0+(-2\pi ) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Sphere
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/c8c7f186ba8769231e9245e0887501f666e56c317fd4f546550202956365b5dc.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+yz,\,y-xz,\,z⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=\sqrt{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+yz,\,y-xz,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨x+yz,\,y-xz,\,z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x(x+yz)+y(y-xz)+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}({x}^{2}+xyz+{y}^{2}-xyz+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 4\pi \cdot (\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  & =8\pi \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/1ee9e32dc5dbe7ba1222a5448ce9ae1227a461a40a36f13e337fce7990263408.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,0,\,-x⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $4$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=4.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{4}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,0,\,-x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{4}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨z,\,0,\,-x⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(xz+0-xz) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Cylinder
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/7ca9996f6d0185d99752ccf5201b5300e0e5149ad674bb9676cf8c716b71a171.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,2y\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $3$ whose base is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,2y\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the left and right sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/320e0c3333aa59f4e856d7d869d6fece09b178ac1abb3acd402621977df9b496.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=3$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,2y\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2(3)\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,6\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =6\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}6\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6{∬}_{D}\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =6{∬}_{D}\sqrt{25-{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{25-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{25-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =6\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[-\frac{1}{3}{(25-{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-4\pi (64-125) \\  & =-4\pi (-61) \\  & =244\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,0,z)=⟨0,\,2(0)\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =244\pi +0 \\  & =244\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/dedd58b5eeeba8b2874c740543132026f95157597dd12ad31fbaa476a3d77c2e.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,{y}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $4$ whose base is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,{y}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the left and right sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/9ffcdd701a8ac6b12cd62773e1cabfd2ce95f9a809e18d087c4bf4f4a22eadb5.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=4$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,{y}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,({4}^{2})(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,16(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =16(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}16(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =16{∬}_{D}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}16{∬}_{D}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =16{∬}_{D}(6-{r}^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r(6-{r}^{2})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}(6r-{r}^{3})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}(6r-{r}^{3})\,\text{d}r \\  & =16\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[3{r}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =32\pi (27-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =32\pi (\frac{27}{4}) \\  & =216\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,0,z)=⟨0,\,{0}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =216\pi +0 \\  & =216\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
